questions.q: According to the chapter, which msdb tables are the primary source of raw backup telemetry (start/end times, type, size, device)?
questions.explain: The chapter's telemetry query joins msdb.dbo.backupset and msdb.dbo.backupmediafamily for backup start/end times, type, size, device, and checksum status.

questions.q: In the chapter's T-SQL Z-score anomaly detection, what thresholds classify a backup's size deviation?
questions.explain: The query flags ABS(z_score) > 3 as CRITICAL_ANOMALY and > 2 as WARNING_ANOMALY, computed against a rolling 30-backup window partitioned by backup type, database, and day of week.

questions.q: A backup duration trend that grows steadily longer over 14 days without a corresponding increase in database size most likely indicates what?
questions.explain: The chapter lists this as the most predictively powerful failure feature: duration growing faster than size signals storage or I/O subsystem degradation before it becomes an incident.

questions.q: How is the XGBoost backup-window scheduling model kept current in the chapter's design?
options: Retrained hourly on a rolling 30-day window
Retrained monthly on a full year of history
Retrained daily on a rolling 7-day window
Retrained weekly on a rolling 90-day window
questions.explain: The chapter states the model is retrained weekly on a rolling 90-day window so it adapts to seasonal patterns, database growth, and application behavior changes without manual intervention.

questions.q: What explicit caution does the chapter give about AI-generated recovery runbooks?
options: They should be piped directly into a shell for speed
They must be reviewed by a human before execution during an actual incident
They should always be executed automatically to minimize RTO
They replace the need for backup validation
questions.explain: The chapter warns not to pipe AI-generated plans directly into a shell: an experienced DBA can validate a generated runbook in two minutes, while the AI accelerates the cognitive work preceding execution.
